why: Concrete, sourced framework with clear risks; A's three-question frame is fine but B is richer and less odd in its closing.
The personal story gives the closing line its weight; A drops the setup so 'the blur' has no referent.
Guess prompt comes before the answer is revealed, so the prediction actually happens.
Says how the rules get shaped together; B's 'not a blank page' line is thinner.
Gives the useful consequence of a mismatch, which completes the spot-check.
'One run at a time' fits the run vocabulary; difference is minor.
Title states the claim, and the slide ends on a short punchy line without repeating it.
Cleaner; A adds a dense parenthetical and a flywheel line that adds little.
Drops the filler 'shape the whole map has had from the start'; tighter.
A's closing line is a loaded, slightly preachy aphorism; B ends on the practical instruction.
Prompts are what was run on M6, so 'prompts' is the more accurate word than 'exercise'.
Clearer: states it's about the pushback and that the compound step reads this session's scrollback.
B ends the point cleanly; A's Module 4 forward reference is a vague tease.
B's 'The training runs on YOUR real work' is a plainer opening than A's 'YOUR real work is the material'.
A's 'The move is the same every time' tells the room it is a repeatable pattern.
B drops the forward reference to Phases 3 and 4, which the room doesn't need yet, so the slide stays on Phase 2.
B adds a concrete description of what the agent does in the loop, so the participant knows what they are reading.
A's 'It often isn't. It's a draft formatted like a decision.' reads with better rhythm; the two versions are otherwise equal.
B's added sentence about not learning the strands here is meta and distracting; A is cleaner.
B has one short instruction, 'Ask these one at a time'. A's wording about the screen and typing along is wordy and confusing.
The title says 'three' and the slide has three items besides the lead, so A's title matches.
B's title says 'Three pressures' and matches the three bullets; A's is vaguer.
B's 'Where the file gets read' says what the slide covers, whereas A just repeats a count.
A's 'what it leaves out' is a more interesting question; B adds MCP detail that hasn't been introduced.
The added 'Three modules in, this is your practice now' line is a narrator telling the student what they feel; B is leaner.
B explains each number (what a taste reversal is, same rules and same task for the leaks), so the story lands. A is terse and the added 'pushed back three times' line is padding.
B drops the redundant 'This is your side-quest lane' opener and gets straight to the instruction.
'A strong candidate for a team PR, after you talk to the team' is hedged and repeats the next bullet; B is tighter.
'Read what Claude proposes' is plainer and fits an instruction to the student; 'Check' is vaguer.
B's point is a real claim about why drawing helps; A's 'see the forest before the trees' is a stock metaphor and says little.
B's title states the lesson as a claim; A's 'Errors stack until a check resets them' is wordier.
B's title is an instruction the student can act on, which suits the neutral, student-controls register.
B names `/context` itself as the oldskool option and points to the built-in status line, so it's clearer and more current.
B says what the output is ('written as an ADR') in plain words.
Naming 'The wall' gives the concept a word, and the rest of the slide can refer back to it.
B's title makes a concrete, pictureable claim and the body then supports it.
'Context window' is the term the body uses; the full name is clearer and consistent.
Closing line adds a memorable, honest takeaway that the rest of the slide sets up.
'Five things' sets expectation and matches the five bullets; a countable title helps the room.
Gives a concrete instruction the participant can act on before the prompt, instead of a vague 'spot what's generic'.
The closing line prevents reading the six phases as a linear pipeline and adds a real insight in few words.
The permission line lowers the stakes for newcomers and supports the experiment framing.
Concrete, actionable and short; A is abstract and tells students nothing to do.
The connective lines orient the participant and explain why the sequence runs this way.
'Alternative' is plainer than 'committed change', which is confusable with a git commit, and the trimmed text is tighter.
